blocks.title: Railways and infrastructure: operating ratios and capital intensity / Charitable giving: donation credits, gifts of securities, and donor advised funds / Apologizing well: ownership without self-abasement
blocks.script:
Company & Economy Analysis, Industry structure, lesson 10: Railways and infrastructure: operating ratios and capital intensity.

Canadian National Railway reported an operating ratio of 61.6 percent for the third quarter of 2025. That single number tells you more about a railway than almost anything else on the income statement, so start there.

Operating ratio is operating expenses divided by revenue. A ratio of 61.6 percent means for every dollar of revenue, 61.6 cents went to running the railway: fuel, labor, equipment, track maintenance. The other 38.4 cents is operating income before interest and tax. Lower is better. This is the inverse of a margin, and that trips people up constantly. A falling operating ratio is improvement. A rising one is deterioration. Say it out loud when you read it, because the instinct to treat big numbers as good will mislead you here.

Now put it against capital intensity. Railways spend enormous sums maintaining track, bridges, and rolling stock just to keep the business standing still. CN's capital expenditure has run close to 19 to 20 percent of revenue in recent years, per its filings, which you can pull from Thomson ONE under the capital expenditure line in the cash flow statement, cross checked against the estimates tab for consensus capex as percent of sales. Compare that to a software company from an earlier lesson, where capex might be 3 or 4 percent of revenue. That gap is the entire story of why railways need decades to earn back an asset and why free cash flow lags net income so visibly in this sector.

The mistake people make is comparing operating ratios across industries, treating a utility's 70 percent ratio as worse than a railway's 62 percent. Different cost structures, different regulatory regimes, different asset lives. Operating ratio is a within-sector tool. It tells you whether CN is running tighter than Canadian Pacific Kansas City or than its own five-year average. It does not tell you whether a railway is a better business than an insurer or a REIT. That comparison needs the full financial plan, not one ratio borrowed from one chart of accounts.

Financial Planning Facts, lesson 39: Charitable giving: donation credits, gifts of securities, and donor advised funds.

Here's the number that changes how you talk to incorporated business owners about giving. If you donate shares with an accrued capital gain directly to a registered charity, the capital gains inclusion rate on that donation drops to zero. Not fifty percent, zero. That rule has been in place federally for years now and it's still the single most underused move in Canadian philanthropy.

Here's the mechanics. Federally, donation credits work on a two tier system for 2025: fifteen percent on the first two hundred dollars donated, twenty nine percent above that, and in some cases thirty three percent on the portion that would otherwise be taxed at the top federal bracket. In Manitoba, the provincial credit is 10.8 percent on the first two hundred dollars and 17.4 percent above that. Combined, you're looking at roughly forty six percent credit on larger gifts.

Now the worked example. A client holds one hundred thousand dollars of public company shares, original cost base twenty thousand dollars. That's an eighty thousand dollar gain. Sell the shares first, then donate cash, and half that gain, forty thousand dollars, gets added to taxable income. Donate the shares directly instead, and the inclusion rate on that gain is zero. Nothing gets added. The client still gets a donation receipt for the full hundred thousand dollars, same as if they'd given cash. For someone in Manitoba's top bracket, avoiding tax on forty thousand dollars of gain saves roughly twenty thousand dollars, on top of the donation credit itself.

The one mistake people make: selling the shares first and then donating the cash proceeds. Once you sell, the gain is locked in and the zero inclusion rate doesn't apply. The shares have to transfer in kind, broker to charity, before any sale happens.

For incorporated owners with lumpy income, a donor advised fund lets them make the gift and get the receipt this year, then recommend grants to specific charities over following years. Useful when there's an unusual spike in corporate dividends or a sale event.

Communication, lesson 39: Apologizing well: ownership without self-abasement.

Business researcher Karen Cates at Northwestern's Kellogg School studied executive apologies and found something counterintuitive: the apologies that rebuilt trust fastest were short, specific, and didn't ask anyone to feel sorry for the apologizer. The ones that failed usually had one of two problems. Either no real ownership, just "mistakes were made." Or too much ownership, spiraling into self-flagellation that made the other person comfort the wronged party, which flips the whole transaction backward.

Here's the structure that works, four parts, roughly fifteen seconds spoken: name the specific action, name the specific impact, state what you're doing differently, stop talking.

Worked example. You're on a nonprofit board. You missed sending board materials 48 hours before the meeting, as your bylaws require, and two members showed up unprepared to vote on a $40,000 grant allocation. Bad version: "I'm so sorry, I've just been completely overwhelmed, I feel terrible, you have no idea how much pressure I'm under." That's 30 seconds about you. Good version: "I sent the board packet six hours before the meeting instead of 48. That meant two of you voted on the grant without time to review it. Starting next cycle, packets go out nine days before, with a calendar reminder I've already set." Fourteen seconds. No adjectives about your feelings. Done.

The one mistake: over-apologizing, which research from Maurice Schweitzer at Wharton on trust repair shows actually reduces perceived competence. Every extra "I'm just so sorry" after the facts are stated reads as either fishing for reassurance or padding time instead of fixing the problem. The listener starts managing your emotions instead of trusting your correction.
talkingPoints: Company & Economy Analysis: Pull CN and CPKC's trailing twelve month operating ratios from Thomson ONE and note which one improved year over year and by how much.

Financial Planning Facts: Pull one client file with appreciated public securities and calculate the tax saved if they donated shares in kind versus cash, using their actual cost base and current bracket.
Communication: Write out, in the four-part structure, an apology for something small you actually did this week. Time yourself saying it out loud. If it runs past 20 seconds, cut adjectives first.

blocks.label: The Ten
blocks.title: Anthropic's record IPO, Quebecor-Telus fight top Canada's business news
blocks.script:
Anthropic priced its initial public offering at 83 US dollars a share overnight, above its targeted range, raising 81 billion dollars. The BBC and CBC both call it the biggest stock market debut on record, valuing the Claude chatbot maker at 1.51 trillion dollars as it starts trading on Nasdaq today. Tailwind: investor demand ran roughly seven times oversubscribed. Headwind: a huge share count frees up fast, and BBC's Simon Jack asks if this pops the AI bubble. An evidence-based advisor says don't chase day-one IPO pops, you're buying hype before fundamentals.

Quebecor is in the news for its 31 billion dollar bid to buy Telus, and even Quebecor's own CEO has conceded the deal squeezes competition from four national players to three. BCE confirmed, per the Globe, it has held talks with Telus about a response, and Prime Minister Carney, at APEC, wouldn't say whether Ottawa can accept losing a major telecom player. Tailwind for Quebecor: a 60 percent premium gets attention. Headwind: regulatory hurdles look steep. An advisor says telecom consolidation plays are binary bets on Ottawa, size positions accordingly.

Telus sits at the center of that fight as the target, warning of serious concerns with the unsolicited offer. Tailwind: a takeover premium lifts the stock near term. Headwind: uncertainty drags on while the special committee reviews. An advisor tells clients not to hold shares purely on deal speculation.

BCE, Telus's rival and possible white knight, is weighing its own move after preliminary talks, the Globe reports. Tailwind: it could block a competitor from growing. Headwind: any BCE counter-bid adds debt to an already leveraged balance sheet. An advisor notes BCE's dividend yield is attractive but watch payout sustainability if a deal emerges.

Bank of Montreal says it has achieved quantum utility, the first Canadian bank to use quantum computing for practical work, the Globe reports. Tailwind: early mover status in a race among global banks. Headwind: practical payoff remains unproven at scale. An advisor says interesting research story, not yet an earnings driver.

Meta is in headlines because Loblaw will let Canadians shop using Meta's Muse AI assistant, the first Canadian retailer to partner directly, per the Globe. Tailwind: positions Meta's AI commerce push globally. Headwind: adoption and trust with shoppers is unproven. An advisor would note this is a small revenue test, not a thesis changer for Meta.

blocks.title: KPMG Breach, RRSP Reform, CIRO Enforcement Today
blocks.script:
Start with KPMG. The firm confirmed yesterday that a cybersecurity breach let an unauthorized party access client tax documents, and it's now contacting affected clients. KPMG hasn't disclosed how many clients, how many files, or how the attacker got in, but it says the data isn't showing up online or being misused. This fits a pattern: the Globe and Mail has reported that at least four major Bay Street law firms, McCarthy Tétrault, Davies Ward Phillips and Vineberg, Bennett Jones, and Borden Ladner Gervais, have had similar breaches. If you have clients who use KPMG for tax prep or corporate structuring, especially incorporated professionals and business owners, this is worth a proactive call. Ask whether their accountant has been in touch, and whether sensitive estate or corporate documents sat in that environment.

On regulation, CIRO, the Canadian Investment Regulatory Organization, issued two notices yesterday. It's holding a settlement hearing for advisor Brady James Rak over gatekeeper obligation allegations, and it sanctioned Arthur Silber in a separate decision. Nothing earth-shaking, but worth knowing if either name surfaces with a client who's moved dealers recently.

The bigger planning story is still Budget 2026's RRSP-for-life proposal. Ottawa wants to merge RRSP, or Registered Retirement Savings Plan, and RRIF, or Registered Retirement Income Fund, rules so clients never have to formally convert at 71. But minimum withdrawals still start at 71, at the same 5.28 percent rate, rising with age. So this is paperwork relief, not a tax break. The one real change: a surviving spouse could become a successor holder more simply. Consultation runs to January 8th, so don't change anyone's retirement plan yet, but flag it to clients turning 71 soon so they don't panic about forced conversions.

blocks.title: Throne Speech, Tesla Ruling, and Siege on Siloam
blocks.script:
A Manitoba judge has ordered the Kinew government to explain, under oath, who decided to cut Tesla out of the province's EV rebate program and why. Court of King's Bench Justice Elissa Neville called it an "exceptional and unusual" remedy, giving the government ten days from November 13 to file a sworn affidavit, with Tesla's lawyers allowed to cross-examine whoever signs it. Tesla has been fighting this since the exclusion began in March 2025, arguing it cost buyers 560,000 dollars and that Premier Kinew's own comments about Elon Musk and tariffs point to a political motive, not a funding decision. The province still says the whole thing is a budget call and unreviewable by the courts. Watch this one, it could get awkward for the government in the legislature.

Speaking of the legislature, Tuesday's throne speech set the table for next year's election. The NDP promised a middle class tax cut starting in 2027, a white collar crime unit, more uniformed police in schools, and two emergency room reopenings including Victoria Hospital next summer. The province says that step down unit will run one nurse per patient. On the business side, Manitoba pledged to match Ottawa's new tax deduction for business and hired a chief mining officer to chase investment. Interim PC leader Konrad Narth called it short on substance.

Steinbach flood victims are getting two million dollars in provincial compensation, though only for one of the two years they were flooded out, in 2024 and 2025.

Winnipeg police have made race based use of force data collection mandatory department wide, a move the service frames as an accountability and transparency step.

blocks.script: Canada has officially lost its measles elimination status, CBC reports, a year after sustained transmission of the same virus strain since October 2024. The country had held that status since 1998. Samira Jeimy from Western University's Schulich School of Medicine says Canada lost its status because two-dose vaccine coverage dropped below the 95 percent threshold required to stop sustained transmission. If you're advising clients on benefits or group health plans, this is the kind of population-level risk that insurers watch. On training: a small new study covered by Outside Online compared 18 young runners, average age 26, against 18 master runners, average age 63. The gap in energy cost widened at the faster speed, from about five percent to about thirteen percent, though the study tested only two moderate speeds.
talkingPoints: Canada lost measles elimination status after vaccine coverage fell below 95 percent.
That's a 27-year run ending, driven by undervaccinated pockets, not the general population.
New small study: older runners burn up to 13 percent more energy at faster paces.
Calf strength training may blunt that age-related efficiency loss.
Worth a reminder to clients: preventive health habits compound like good portfolios.

blocks.title: New Teen Guidance, Parental Leave Numbers Worth Knowing
blocks.script: The Canadian Paediatric Society issued new guidance this month urging doctors to routinely ask teen patients about healthy relationships and dating violence. The society says one third of Canadian teens experience some form of physical, psychological, sexual, or technology-related abuse in relationships, including online tracking by a partner. For clients with teenagers, this is a cue to normalize that conversation at home too, not just in the doctor's office. On the financial side, Employment Insurance parental benefits for 2026 pay 55 percent of average insurable earnings, up to 729 dollars a week, for standard leave up to 40 shared weeks. Extended leave pays 33 percent, up to 437 dollars a week, over 69 shared weeks. The Canada Child Benefit for the current year runs up to 7,787 dollars annually per child under six, phasing out as household income rises.

blocks.script:
Company & Economy Analysis, Valuation reps, lesson 9: Scenario valuation: bull, base, bear, and probability weighting.

A single discounted cash flow number is a lie dressed up as precision. You put in one growth rate, one margin assumption, one discount rate, and the model spits out a figure that looks exact to the penny. It never is. The honest fix is to build three cases and weight them by how likely you actually think they are.

Take a name like Canadian Natural Resources. In the base case, say you assume West Texas Intermediate averages 70 US dollars a barrel through the forecast window, production grows modestly, and you land on a fair value of 48 dollars a share. In the bull case, oil runs to 85, free cash flow jumps, and your value comes out near 62 dollars. In the bear case, oil slides to 55 on demand weakness, and your value drops to 34 dollars. Now assign probabilities. Not fifty-fifty-zero, that is lazy. Say 25 percent bull, 50 percent base, 25 percent bear. The weighted value is point two five times 62, plus point five times 48, plus point two five times 34. That is 15.5 plus 24 plus 8.5, which comes to 48 dollars. In this case the weighted figure lands close to your base case, which tells you the distribution is roughly symmetric. If the weighted number drifts far from the base case, that is the real signal, it means your downside or upside is doing more work than your gut assumed.

The one mistake people make is building three cases that only differ in the growth rate while holding margins and multiples fixed. That is not three scenarios, it is one scenario dressed three times. Bull and bear need their own margin assumptions and their own exit multiples, not just a faster top line.

This tells you the range of reasonable outcomes and where the market's current price sits inside that range. It cannot tell you which scenario will actually happen. That is still a judgment call, not a model output. Analysis first, technicals second, sector comparison third, same order as always.

Financial Planning Facts, lesson 38: RRIF: minimum withdrawals, the age 65 pension credit, and the age of the younger spouse election.

Here is the thing most people over 71 get wrong about their RRIF, registered retirement income fund. They think the minimum withdrawal is fixed. It is not. It is a percentage of the December 31 balance from the prior year, and the percentage climbs every year you age.

For 2026, if the account holder is 71, the minimum factor is 5.28 percent. At 75, it jumps to 5.82 percent. At 80, it is 6.82 percent. At 90, it is 11.92 percent. These factors are set by the Income Tax Act and they do not change with interest rates, so say that to a client who thinks they are tied to bond yields. They are not.

Here is the worked example. A client turns 72 in 2026. Their RRIF held 500,000 dollars on December 31, 2025. The factor at age 72 is 5.40 percent. That means the 2026 minimum withdrawal is 27,000 dollars, and no tax is withheld at source on amounts up to the minimum. Over the minimum, withholding kicks in.

Now the age 65 pension credit. Once someone turns 65, RRIF withdrawals qualify as eligible pension income, which means up to 2,000 dollars of it is sheltered by the pension income credit federally, worth roughly 300 dollars in tax saved, and Manitoba has its own pension income amount on top of that on the provincial return. RRSP withdrawals do not qualify. This is one reason to convert part of an RRSP to a RRIF before age 71 if someone wants to use that credit earlier.

The one mistake: using the account holder's age for the minimum factor when the spouse is younger. You can elect, at the time the RRIF is set up, to base the minimum on the younger spouse's age instead. That election is made once, in writing, with the carrier, and it is irrevocable. A couple with a 70 year old RRIF holder and a 60 year old spouse can cut the minimum withdrawal nearly in half by electing the younger age, which matters a lot for income splitting and for deferring tax.

Communication, lesson 38: Humour: when it works in a professional setting and when it costs you.

Jennifer Aaker at Stanford ran the numbers on this. Her research with Naomi Bagdonas found that executives who use humour well are seen as 23 percent more competent and 25 percent more admired by their teams than those who don't, based on surveys across hundreds of leaders. That's a real, measurable business outcome, not a personality trait.

Here's the mechanism. Self-deprecating humour aimed at your own minor flaws signals confidence, because only someone secure enough can joke about their own slip. You open a board meeting with "I spent twenty minutes before this call trying to unmute myself, so if nothing else, I've lowered expectations early." That's three seconds, it's true, and it makes the room relax before you ask for something hard.

Now the version that costs you. Humour that punches at someone else in the room, even gently, even as a callback to an inside joke, creates an outgroup. A 2007 study by Robert Lynch and colleagues on humour styles found that "aggressive humour", jokes at another's expense, correlates with lower trust ratings from observers, even when the target laughs along. On a nonprofit board, where you're one of several voices and not the final decision maker, that's expensive. You're not the hero of that room, the cause is, and a joke that makes another board member the punchline undercuts the frame you're supposed to be holding for them.

The single mistake: timing it to the content instead of the room. People reach for a joke right when they're nervous, which is usually right before the ask or the hard number. That's the exact moment the room is listening hardest, and a joke there reads as deflection, not confidence.

Self-deprecating, early, about yourself only. Never aimed at a colleague, a client, or the room's mood. Never right before the ask.

blocks.label: The Ten
blocks.title: Nvidia, Telus Lead A Pension-Heavy News Day
blocks.script:
Nvidia posted fiscal third quarter revenue guidance above Wall Street estimates, giving markets relief after a rout that had erased roughly two trillion dollars in value from its October peak. Shares rallied about four per cent after hours. The tailwind is that AI chip demand still looks healthy. The headwind is governance: the board confirmed on an investor call it will not rehire Jensen Huang despite his public openness to return. An evidence based advisor would say one earnings beat does not override a diversification plan.

Telus, the Vancouver based telecom Darren Entwistle built from a Western carrier into a national player, is now a takeover target as Quebecor pursues a bid. Prime Minister Carney, per the Globe, stayed mum on whether Ottawa would let the sector lose a national player, saying only that his government favours more competition. The tailwind is political pressure for a resolution. The headwind is prolonged uncertainty. An advisor would say event driven stocks need a sized position, not a bet.

L3Harris Technologies installed the router blamed for last week's nationwide ground stop, and the Federal Aviation Administration has now paused further installations while it investigates. The tailwind is a deep air traffic modernization contract pipeline. The headwind is Senate Democrats demanding answers before new work proceeds. An advisor would say single contractor headline risk rarely changes a long term thesis.

Hewlett Packard Enterprise, which owns router maker Juniper, says its equipment worked as configured when the outage hit seventeen of twenty two air traffic centres. The tailwind is HPE's networking business keeps winning critical infrastructure work. The headwind is reputational exposure even while disclaiming fault. An advisor would say wait for the root cause before reading much into the stock.

GE Vernova, the power equipment business spun off from General Electric, has formed an alliance to supply technology for the thirty billion dollar undersea NATO-L transmission line linking Canada and Europe. The tailwind is a multi decade grid buildout order book. The headwind is years of permitting risk before revenue lands. An advisor would say treat mega project headlines as thesis support, not a signal to trade.

OMERS has teamed with Transmission Developers Infrastructure to bid on an underwater electricity line from the Darlington nuclear plant into Toronto's Port Lands. The tailwind is regulated returns matching pension liabilities. The headwind is construction delays common to major transmission builds. An advisor would say this is exactly the patient capital role pension funds exist for.

La Caisse is in talks for a stake in Bain Capital's Bridge Data Centres, a Singapore based operator, with the size of the stake still being negotiated. The tailwind is AI driven data centre demand. The headwind is stretched valuations after a frantic year of deals. An advisor would say pension scale diversification is reasonable, but don't chase the same multiples personally.

blocks.title: Foreign Property Threshold Doubles, Insolvencies Stay High
blocks.script:
Start with the one that affects almost every cross-border or snowbird client file. Globe Advisor reports Budget 2026 proposes to raise the T1135 foreign property reporting threshold from $100,000 to $200,000, and the simplified-reporting ceiling from under $250,000 to under $500,000, for taxation years ending after 2026. That change alone would exempt approximately one-third of all current filers from the obligation to file, something like 240,000 taxpayers. It does not apply to this year's return, only tax years ending after 2026, so do not let clients skip their current T1135 on the strength of this headline.

Household stress is the backdrop. Wealth Professional's new data shows Canadian consumer insolvencies have stayed above 36,000 for a third straight quarter, the highest sustained pace since 2009, and that is landing right as holiday budgets climb and financial insecurity rises, especially among younger clients. If you have incorporated business owners or physicians in a life transition right now, divorce, retirement, practice sale, this is the moment to flag cash flow before they lever up for the season.

On fraud, deepfake attacks are climbing, hitting 44% of anti-fraud teams surveyed, with only a sliver rating their firm well prepared. Pair that with Capital One's finding that Canadians still trust banks over AI chatbots for money advice, and you have a good opening line with clients worried about scams: the trust gap is your selling point, use it.

The Quebecor-Telus story is already on your radar, but here is your angle: Telus's board warned the eighty-one-dollar bid would shrink dividends, citing 4.1 times leverage in the combined company. If you hold Telus for income in client portfolios, that yield compression risk needs a conversation now, not after a deal closes.

On the watch list today: the Bank of Canada's next rate decision lands December 9, its only remaining call of the year after October's quarter-point hike to 2.50%. Also smaller industry moves: BMO added six new ETFs, and Knowledge Bureau opened a new tax planning certificate for CFPs.

blocks.label: Manitoba & Winnipeg
blocks.title: Throne Speech Tax Cuts, Record Wait Times, Prairie Health Risks
blocks.script:
The throne speech is the story your clients will be asking about today. Premier Wab Kinew delivered his fourth and final throne speech before next year's election, and the headline is a "mega-deduction" style middle-class tax cut coming in the spring budget. He didn't give you a number yet, but he framed it plainly: "the rich obviously have a lot of folks helping them, so we think it's the middle class's turn to get some help." For business clients, there's more: the province will match Ottawa's new federal tax deduction for business, and Manitoba has created a new chief mining officer role, filled by industry veteran Stacy Kennedy, aimed at cutting red tape for mining investment. On health, the government is promising the Victoria Hospital emergency room back open next summer, a second new ER in Eriksdale by next fall, free shingles vaccines for seniors 65 to 79 and immunocompromised adults starting in July, funding for police in schools, and new rules banning artificial intelligence generated images in real estate listings. The Opposition called it short on substance, and columnist Tom Brodbeck points out that reopening Victoria's ER won't fix the underlying wait time crunch.

That crunch is real and it's getting worse. A CBC analysis out today found Manitobans can wait nine months or longer for an ultrasound, fifteen months for a CT scan, and ten months for an MRI depending on where the scan gets sent, with one doctor calling the backlog worse than it has ever been. That is a talking point for any client with aging parents or chronic conditions, and it is pushing more Manitobans toward private cross-border imaging.

blocks.script:
The biggest story for you today sits in Shenzhen. Prime Minister Mark Carney met with Donald Trump on the sidelines of the APEC summit, a meeting the Prime Minister's Office says ran nearly twenty minutes, with no detailed readout yet, the Globe and Mail reports. Carney also sat down with Xi Jinping, and Ottawa announced China will extend tariff relief for two years on four hundred million dollars of Canadian exports, including pork and seafood, while Canada extends and expands remission on some Chinese steel and aluminum. Carney pitched the Pacific Link pipeline to business leaders at the summit, framing Canada as a reliable energy and food supplier for Asian markets. He's also expected to discuss trade ties with Mexico's Sheinbaum while there. Back home, trade officials tell CBC that talks between Canada and the US have quietly ramped up, with weekly meetings between negotiating teams.

On the fiscal side, the Parliamentary Budget Officer's assessment of the 2026 budget flags public debt charges as Ottawa's fastest growing expense, saying the government, quote, spends more, invests more and borrows more. Worth watching if you're positioning fixed income for clients concerned about federal borrowing costs.

In committee work, Conservatives pressed Invest in Canada's new chair, Dominic Barton, over potential conflicts tied to his Rio Tinto board role, while Liberals moved to limit debate on changes to the medical assistance in dying law, drawing pushback from opposition MPs wanting more study.

And after this morning's throne speech, Premier Wab Kinew now heads toward a provincial election with his tax cut and health commitments as the centerpiece of his pitch to Manitobans.

blocks.label: Parenting
blocks.title: Screen Time Surprise, and Less Paranoid Parenting
blocks.script:
An eight-year Finnish study followed children from the PANIC research project and found something unexpected: more accumulated screen time was linked to better cognitive processing by adolescence, not worse. Accumulating less unsupervised physical activity and more screen time from childhood to adolescence was associated with better cognition in adolescence, and the researchers say screen time can support cognitive processing. The catch is what children actually do on screens, coding or problem-solving appears to matter more than raw hours, and researchers stress this is association, not proof of causation.

Separately, a Globe and Mail essay this week pushes back against what the writer calls paranoid parenting, arguing kids need unsupervised freedom to build independence. For clients raising young families, it is a useful counterweight to headlines that treat every screen minute as damage.

blocks.title: Raiders Fall, Jets Slip, Scheifele Still Climbing
blocks.script:
Start with the Raiders, since that's your priority team. Las Vegas lost 21-13 to Seattle on Sunday, falling to 4 and 6. Rookie Fernando Mendoza made his first career start at quarterback and got sacked six times, per ESPN and CBS Sports. The headline moment came late: trailing by 8, the Raiders tried a trick kickoff play to preserve a timeout, sending the ball out of bounds on purpose, but Seahawks receiver Tory Horton batted it and drew a flag the Raiders couldn't actually use. The NFL has now flexed Las Vegas's week 12 game at Cleveland to Sunday Night Football on NBC, November 29th. Before that, they're at Denver this Sunday.

Elsewhere in the NFL, Detroit's Dan Campbell confirmed star edge rusher Aidan Hutchinson is out for the season with a torn ACL, suffered celebrating a sack in Germany against New England. The Patriots have their own problem: quarterback Drake Maye is expected to miss extended time, maybe the rest of the year, with an ankle injury from that same game.

Now your Jets. Ottawa snapped Winnipeg's six-game win streak Monday, winning 2-1 as Boucher scored the winner in his NHL debut, and the Senators now sit atop the Atlantic. Still, Mark Scheifele keeps rewriting the franchise record book, fresh off first-star-of-the-week honours, having passed Dale Hawerchuk for Winnipeg's all-time points lead, per CBC.

blocks.title: Goodwill and intangibles: what an impairment actually signals / Retirement income sequencing: which account to draw first and why / Networking: introductions that people remember
blocks.script:
Company & Economy Analysis, Statement forensics, lesson 8: Goodwill and intangibles: what an impairment actually signals.

Kraft Heinz wrote down nine point three billion dollars of goodwill in one quarter back in 2019, tied to its Kraft and Oscar Mayer brands. The stock fell down over eight percent the next trading day. People read that as the business collapsing. It did not collapse. What collapsed was an accounting estimate made years earlier, when Kraft and Heinz merged and somebody priced the combined brand value too high.

Here is what goodwill actually is. When a company buys another company for more than the fair value of its identifiable assets, the excess sits on the balance sheet as goodwill. It is not cash, it is not a factory, it is the premium paid for reputation, customer relationships, expected synergies. Every year under United States accounting rules, management has to test whether that premium still holds up. If projected cash flows from that acquired business fall below what was assumed at purchase, they write it down. That write-down is the impairment.

The mistake people make is treating an impairment as new bad news about the future. It is not. It is a confession about the past, specifically about a price paid years ago that turned out to be wrong. The cash left the building at acquisition. The impairment changes earnings per share and book value, but it does not touch current cash flow. Check this on Thomson ONE in the cash flow statement: impairment charges get added back above the operating cash flow line, because they are non-cash.

What it does tell you, reliably, is that management's own forecast for that business segment has deteriorated enough to breach a threshold. That is useful. It is a lagging confirmation that a prior deal underperformed, and it can flag where a segment is struggling before the segment's own revenue line shows it clearly. What it cannot tell you is current competitive position, current demand, or whether the core business is healthy. For that you still need the revenue and margin trends underneath.

Always separate the impairment line from operating performance before you judge the quarter.

Financial Planning Facts, lesson 37: Retirement income sequencing: which account to draw first and why.

The biggest mistake in retirement income planning is drawing RRSP or RRIF money last, because it feels like the one you're "saving." That instinct costs clients real dollars, and here's why.

Your accounts aren't equal. A Tax-Free Savings Account, or TFSA, grows and comes out with zero tax, ever. A non-registered account only gets taxed on the growth portion each year. An RRSP or RRIF, once you convert at 71, gets taxed at full marginal rate on every dollar withdrawn, and it also keeps growing, pushing future withdrawals into higher brackets and triggering Old Age Security clawback.

The general sequencing logic for 2026: spend non-registered investments first, because their tax drag is lowest and you want to preserve tax sheltered room elsewhere. Then draw some RRSP or RRIF, deliberately, even before you need the cash, to smooth your income across retirement rather than hitting a wall at 71. Save TFSA for last, because it's the only account that never triggers clawback and never triggers tax, so it's your most flexible buffer for large one-time needs or late-life top-ups.

Worked example. A retired Manitoba physician, age 62, has 900,000 dollars in a RRIF-eligible RRSP, 200,000 in non-registered investments, and 150,000 in a TFSA. If she spends TFSA first, by 71 her RRSP has kept compounding at say 5 percent, swelling past 1.3 million, forcing minimum withdrawals that push her into OAS clawback territory once she's 65 and collecting it. Instead, drawing 40,000 a year from the RRSP starting at 62, using lower brackets now while she has room, and topping up with non-registered funds, keeps her lifetime tax bill lower and her TFSA intact for flexibility at 80 or 85.

The one mistake: treating the RRSP as the account you touch last. It's usually the account you should start drawing from early, on purpose, before the government forces the pace with mandatory minimums.

Communication, lesson 37: Networking: introductions that people remember.

Harvard Business School researcher Alison Wood Brooks ran a study on conversations and found something specific: people remember the questions you asked them far more than the facts you told them about yourself. Her 2017 paper, published in Management Science, tracked speed daters and job interviewers. The people rated as most likeable asked, on average, nine more follow up questions per conversation than the least likeable ones. Not more questions overall. Follow up questions. The kind that prove you were listening to the last answer, not waiting for your turn.

Here is the mistake almost everyone makes at a networking event or board dinner: they lead with their own credential. "I'm an advisor, I work with founders on exits, I also sit on two nonprofit boards." That's a business card read aloud. Nobody remembers a business card. What they remember is the one moment you made them talk about something specific and then asked a second question about it.

Worked example. You meet someone at a board function who says, "I run operations for a mid-size logistics company." Weak move: "That's great, I work with a lot of operators too." Strong move: "What's the thing that broke this year that you didn't expect to?" They answer, say, "Our freight costs jumped 22 percent after a carrier consolidation, per the numbers our CFO showed the board in March." Now the follow up: "Did that change who you're negotiating contracts with, or just the price?" That second question is the one they'll bring up to their spouse that night, not your title.

The single mistake: treating the opener as the whole interaction instead of the first half of it. One good question with no follow up is just small talk with better phrasing.
talkingPoints: Company & Economy Analysis: Pull one company from Thomson ONE that reported a goodwill impairment in the last three years. Compare its operating cash flow the quarter of the impairment versus the quarter before, and confirm whether it moved at all.

Financial Planning Facts: Pull one client's current account balances across TFSA, non-registered, and RRSP or RRIF. Estimate what their RRSP balance will be at age 71 if untouched, using a simple 5 percent growth assumption, and flag whether that creates a clawback risk.

Communication: At your next event or call this week, pick one person and ask a specific question about their work, then ask one follow up question before you say anything about yourself. Notice if they lean in or check their phone.

What it cannot tell you is current competitive position, current demand, or whether the core business is healthy. For that you still need the revenue and margin trends underneath.

Always separate the impairment line from operating performance before you judge the quarter.

lessons.label: Financial Planning Facts
lessons.title: Retirement income sequencing: which account to draw first and why
lessons.script:
The biggest mistake in retirement income planning is drawing RRSP or RRIF money last, because it feels like the one you're "saving." That instinct costs clients real dollars, and here's why.

Your accounts aren't equal. A Tax-Free Savings Account, or TFSA, grows and comes out with zero tax, ever. A non-registered account only gets taxed on the growth portion each year. An RRSP or RRIF, once you convert at 71, gets taxed at full marginal rate on every dollar withdrawn, and it also keeps growing, pushing future withdrawals into higher brackets and triggering Old Age Security clawback.

The general sequencing logic for 2026: spend non-registered investments first, because their tax drag is lowest and you want to preserve tax sheltered room elsewhere. Then draw some RRSP or RRIF, deliberately, even before you need the cash, to smooth your income across retirement rather than hitting a wall at 71. Save TFSA for last, because it's the only account that never triggers clawback and never triggers tax, so it's your most flexible buffer for large one-time needs or late-life top-ups.

Worked example. A retired Manitoba physician, age 62, has 900,000 dollars in a RRIF-eligible RRSP, 200,000 in non-registered investments, and 150,000 in a TFSA. If she spends TFSA first, by 71 her RRSP has kept compounding at say 5 percent, swelling past 1.3 million, forcing minimum withdrawals that push her into OAS clawback territory once she's 65 and collecting it. Instead, drawing 40,000 a year from the RRSP starting at 62, using lower brackets now while she has room, and topping up with non-registered funds, keeps her lifetime tax bill lower and her TFSA intact for flexibility at 80 or 85.

The one mistake: treating the RRSP as the account you touch last. It's usually the account you should start drawing from early, on purpose, before the government forces the pace with mandatory minimums.
lessons.task: Pull one client's current account balances across TFSA, non-registered, and RRSP or RRIF. Estimate what their RRSP balance will be at age 71 if untouched, using a simple 5 percent growth assumption, and flag whether that creates a clawback risk.

lessons.label: Communication
lessons.title: Networking: introductions that people remember
lessons.script:
Harvard Business School researcher Alison Wood Brooks ran a study on conversations and found something specific: people remember the questions you asked them far more than the facts you told them about yourself. Her 2017 paper, published in Management Science, tracked speed daters and job interviewers. The people rated as most likeable asked, on average, nine more follow up questions per conversation than the least likeable ones. Not more questions overall. Follow up questions. The kind that prove you were listening to the last answer, not waiting for your turn.

Here is the mistake almost everyone makes at a networking event or board dinner: they lead with their own credential. "I'm an advisor, I work with founders on exits, I also sit on two nonprofit boards." That's a business card read aloud. Nobody remembers a business card. What they remember is the one moment you made them talk about something specific and then asked a second question about it.

Worked example. You meet someone at a board function who says, "I run operations for a mid-size logistics company." Weak move: "That's great, I work with a lot of operators too." Strong move: "What's the thing that broke this year that you didn't expect to?" They answer, say, "Our freight costs jumped 22 percent after a carrier consolidation, per the numbers our CFO showed the board in March." Now the follow up: "Did that change who you're negotiating contracts with, or just the price?" That second question is the one they'll bring up to their spouse that night, not your title.

The single mistake: treating the opener as the whole interaction instead of the first half of it. One good question with no follow up is just small talk with better phrasing.
lessons.task: At your next event or call this week, pick one person and ask a specific question about their work, then ask one follow up question before you say anything about yourself. Notice if they lean in or check their phone.
lessons.drill: Record yourself doing three fake introductions, thirty seconds each, to an empty chair. Score each one: did you ask a question before introducing yourself, yes or no, and did you ask a follow up to their imagined answer, yes or no. Good looks like two yeses on all three, with zero sentences that start with "I".

blocks.script:
Quebecor is the biggest name in business news right now. The Montreal media and telecom company, owner of Videotron, has tabled an unsolicited thirty one billion dollar bid for rival Telus. The Globe and Mail reports CEO Pierre Karl Péladeau argues the combined company would be better positioned to compete globally. The tailwind is scale and spectrum. The headwind is a wall of regulatory approval, since Ottawa has spent years pushing for four strong players, not three. An evidence based advisor would tell you this is event driven noise, don't trade telecom holdings on takeover headlines before any deal actually closes.

Telus is the target, and not a willing one. The Globe reports the unsolicited pitch is being called full of holes by rival leadership. The tailwind for Telus shareholders is a takeover premium lifting the share price today. The headwind is months of uncertainty that could weigh on operations regardless of outcome. An advisor says don't chase the premium, wait for a firm deal before repositioning.

The Bank of Canada is on the watch list, and the governor is the story. Tiff Macklem confirmed he won't seek a second term, officially opening the search for his successor, with BlackRock's Jean Boivin seen as an early favourite, per the Globe. The tailwind is a calm, telegraphed transition. The headwind is uncertainty over whether a new governor shifts the bank's rate bias. An advisor says leadership changes rarely move your portfolio, stay diversified regardless of who sits in the chair.

Nvidia, the dominant AI chip maker, is in commentary today over culture, not silicon, with the Globe questioning strongman leadership patterns around founder control. The tailwind is its grip on AI hardware demand. The headwind is concentration risk tied to one personality. An advisor says don't let conviction in a single stock override a diversified plan, even a market darling.

blocks.title: Incorporation Stalls, New Exemption Lands, IPO Opens
blocks.script:
Start with the number that matters most for your incorporated business owner clients. Budget 2026 proposes a new Canada Growth Incentive giving up to fifteen million dollars in tax-free capital gains, per person, per business, on qualifying shares. Advisor dot ca reports the rules are tight: a qualifying share must be issued by a Canadian-controlled private corporation, the combined carrying value of that corporation and related corporations must not exceed $100m at issuance, and the share must be held for at least 36 consecutive months before disposition. That means most existing business owners won't qualify right away, only new share issuances after budget day. Wealth Professional's advisor panel confirms this changes how founders and investors think about every new share acquired, though eligibility requirements mean it won't apply to most business owners. For your incorporated clients who are planning a sale in five or ten years, this is worth a conversation now about share structure, because the exemption applies to individuals directly, not through a holding company.

Separately, advisor incorporation itself remains stuck. CIRO told the Advocis symposium last week that a rule allowing securities-licensed advisors to incorporate is "some ways away", with the regulator's real goal being to build a model that's "evergreen" amid further developments. Don't tell clients this is imminent. It isn't.

Anthropic's IPO is the other story to watch. Wealth Professional notes the Claude maker's offering brings frontier artificial intelligence exposure to individual investors for the first time, so expect calls this week from clients wanting in, and expect volatility around it.

blocks.script:
Manitoba's government says it has cut spending on nursing and health-care aide agencies by nearly fifty million dollars, a move the province is framing as money redirected from private contractors back toward public front-line care. For you, the read is simple: watch for whether Shared Health follows through, because past attempts to pull back from these agencies have been reversed within months when staffing gaps reopened.

On the same health file, Manitoba is close to the top of the country for flu activity right now, and that is adding pressure to Winnipeg emergency rooms already stretched thin, which makes the timing of an agency spending cut worth watching closely with clients in health-adjacent sectors.

The province is also creating an independent disability advocate role, a response to a human rights complaint, giving Manitobans with disabilities a dedicated office to escalate concerns outside the health bureaucracy.

On the international side, Manitoba has formally joined the Organisation Internationale de la Francophonie, the global body of French-speaking nations, and took part in its first summit this past week in Cambodia. The province is pitching this as a door to new commercial and cultural ties, worth flagging if you have clients in trade or export-facing business.

Manitoba also named its first chief mining officer, Stacy Kennedy, who leaves a director role at Vale, with a mandate to accelerate growth in the sector. If you have exposure to junior miners or exploration names tied to Manitoba, that is a signal the province wants to move faster on permitting and investment attraction.

In Winnipeg, the street census got underway this week as the federal government pledged a billion dollars toward ending homelessness in the city, a number that will shape how municipal and provincial budgets get built next year.

And a fifth soldier has died from the CFB Wainwright fire, a loss being felt across the Manitoba military community given how many reservists and families here have ties to that base.

blocks.script:
Company & Economy Analysis, Macro & rates, lesson 8: Housing and household debt: Canada's specific exposure and the policy levers.

Canada's household debt to disposable income ratio sat at roughly 174 percent as of Statistics Canada's second quarter 2025 release. That means for every dollar a household takes home after tax, it owes about a dollar seventy four. Compare that to the United States, where the equivalent figure is closer to 100 percent. That gap is the story, and it did not happen by accident.

Here is the mechanism. Canadian mortgages are not thirty year fixed like the typical American loan. Most are five year terms, amortized over twenty five or thirty years, and they renew. When the Bank of Canada moved its policy rate from near zero in 2022 up to 5 percent by mid 2023, every household renewing a mortgage during that window faced a payment shock, not a gradual one. The Bank of Canada itself flagged in its Financial Stability Report that a meaningful share of mortgages originated in 2020 and 2021, at rock bottom rates, were set to renew into materially higher rates through 2025 and 2026.

Worked example. Take a 500,000 dollar mortgage, 25 year amortization, taken out in 2021 at 2 percent. Monthly payment is roughly 2,118 dollars. That same balance renewing in 2025 at 4.5 percent, after some principal paydown, pushes the payment to around 2,600 dollars. That is close to a 500 dollar monthly increase, on one mortgage. Multiply that across the roughly 1.2 million mortgages Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation estimated would renew in 2025 and 2026, and you see why this is a macro issue, not a household one.

The mistake people make is treating a rate cut as the fix. It helps at the margin, but the renewal wall was baked in at origination. The policy lever that matters more is amortization flexibility, lenders quietly extending amortizations back out, which the Office of the Superintendent of Financial Institutions has tracked and reported on.

What this tells you: household debt levels explain fragility, not timing. It cannot tell you when a correction happens, only where the stress concentrates.

Financial Planning Facts, lesson 36: Inheritance: what is taxable, what is not, and the planning that follows.

Here is the thing most clients get backwards. In Canada, an inheritance itself is not taxed as income to the person receiving it. There is no inheritance tax in this country. What gets taxed happens before the money reaches you, at the estate level, through what's called a deemed disposition on the deceased's final tax return.

When someone dies, the Canada Revenue Agency treats them as if they sold everything they owned at fair market value, the moment before death. That triggers capital gains on things like non-registered investments, a cottage, or shares in a private corporation. It also collapses RRSPs and RRIFs into income on that final return, unless there's a surviving spouse or a qualifying dependent to roll it to.

Here's a worked example. Your client's father dies in 2026 owning a cottage worth 600,000 dollars, originally bought for 150,000 dollars. That's a 450,000 dollar capital gain. For 2026, the inclusion rate is 50 percent on the first 250,000 dollars of gains in the year, and the government has confirmed the rate stays at 50 percent going forward after the proposed increase to two-thirds was cancelled in January 2025. So 225,000 dollars is added to the father's income on his terminal return, taxed at his marginal rate that year. The estate pays that tax, then your client inherits the cottage with a new, stepped-up cost base of 600,000 dollars. The inheritance itself, once that tax is settled, comes to your client tax-free.

The one mistake people make: they assume if they inherit a non-registered account or property, they personally owe tax on receiving it. They don't. The estate already paid, or the estate owes before probate closes. What your client needs to ask isn't "will I be taxed," it's "did the estate have enough liquidity to cover the deemed disposition," especially with real estate or private company shares where there's no cash sitting there to pay the bill.

Communication, lesson 36: The follow up: what to send after a meeting and when.

Robert Cialdini ran a study with waiters at a restaurant. The ones who left a second mint on the table, after already leaving one, saw tips jump by 23 percent. Same food, same service, just a small unexpected follow through after the moment people expected the interaction to be over. That is what a good follow up does. It is not a recap. It is the second mint.

Most advisors send the recap anyway. "Great meeting today, here is what we discussed." That email gets skimmed in four seconds and deleted. It adds zero information the client did not already have, because they were sitting in the room.

Here is the version that works. Within two hours of the meeting, not the next morning, send three things only. One sentence naming the specific decision or tension that came up, in the client's own words if you can. One concrete next step with a date attached, not "soon," an actual date: "I will send the revised allocation by Thursday the 20th." And one line that shows you were listening for them, not performing for them: something about their daughter's wedding, their business sale, the thing that was actually on their mind underneath the numbers.

Example. Client meeting ends at 2pm. You discussed moving 400,000 dollars from a taxable account into a donor advised fund before year end, partly for the 2025 deduction, partly because his daughter's wedding is draining cash in the spring. At 3:40pm you send: "You were weighing the DAF move against keeping liquidity for Sarah's wedding in May. I will have two scenarios, full 400k now versus a split with 150k held back, by Wednesday the 19th." That is nineteen seconds to read and it proves you were in the room with him, not just at it.

The one mistake: sending the follow up the same day but making it generic, or waiting three days and making it specific. Speed and specificity both have to show up, or the client reads it as a template.

blocks.title: Quebecor Stuns Telus, Intel Faces Lawsuits
blocks.script:
Quebecor just launched the biggest Canadian deal story in years. It's offering roughly 31 billion dollars, about 19.45 dollars a share in cash and stock, a 60 percent premium, to buy Telus. The tailwind for Quebecor is scale and a combined network. The headwind is enormous: Telus itself flagged serious regulatory and governance risk. An evidence-based advisor says don't trade on takeover rumours, hold your index weight and let the deal process play out.

Telus is the target here, reviewing the unsolicited bid through a special committee chaired by John Manley. The tailwind is the 60 percent premium on the table. The headwind is that saying yes could take years through competition and telecom regulators, and may never close. An advisor tells clients: a premium on paper is not cash in hand, don't reprice your plan on an unconfirmed deal.

Intel is now facing a shareholder class action after its stock plunged 29 percent, with the Globe and BBC both reporting the suit claims the chipmaker hid how badly PC sales were slowing. The tailwind is Intel's ongoing turnaround push in foundry and AI chips. The headwind is litigation risk layered on top of a demand slump. An advisor says single stock headline risk like this is exactly why concentrated bets need a stop-loss plan, not conviction.

Canaccord Genuity is going private. Chief executive Dan Daviau is leading a 1.6 billion dollar buyout, contingent on selling its UK wealth arm to Centerbridge Partners and Mubadala for about 1.55 billion dollars. The tailwind is certainty, two thirds of votes plus a third already locked in support. The headwind is this is Daviau's second attempt after one failed in 2023. An advisor tells clients holding Canaccord shares: take the cash offer seriously, don't hold out for a higher bid that may not come.

blocks.title: Budget's New $15 Million Exemption, Wealthsimple's Branch Gambit
blocks.script:
The biggest thing on your desk this morning is a new capital gains exemption buried in Budget 2026, and Wealth Professional's advisor survey shows it's splitting books right down the middle. Budget 2026 proposes to exempt up to $15 million in capital gains per person, per business, on qualifying shares issued on or after budget day, November 5. It's being called the Canada Growth Incentive. For advisors whose clients are founders, early employees and tech professionals, it changes how they treat every new share a client acquires. But before you get excited for your incorporated physician clients, check the exclusions. Consulting businesses are excluded, as are professional practices in accounting, law, medicine, engineering and architecture, and any business whose principal asset is the reputation or skill of its employees. That likely rules out most medical professional corporations. And it's not law yet: draft legislation for the exemption was not released with the budget. Flag it, don't promise it.

On the retail landscape, the Globe reports Wealthsimple is capitalizing on bank branch closures. Cash deposits nearly quadrupled between March and October, when they reached 26 million dollars in one month, with total transactions amounting to more than 130 million dollars. One in five of those deposits came from smaller communities, which matters for how you think about competition outside Winnipeg's core.

Advisor incorporation reform is still parked. Per Advisor.ca, CIRO told an Advocis event the aim is an "evergreen" model, but it's "some ways away." Don't tell incorporated advisor clients to expect a fix soon.

blocks.title: Wainwright Death, Road Safety Rally, Kinew's Re-Election Push
blocks.script:
A fifth soldier has died from injuries in the CFB Wainwright fire. The Department of National Defence confirmed Private William Douglas Dal Bianco died on November 13 at an Ontario hospital, more than three weeks after the October 17 blaze at the Alberta base. The military said 24 of the 38 members injured in the fire remain in hospital, while 14 have been released. This isn't a Manitoba story directly, but several of you have ties to military families here, and it's the kind of news that comes up at the dinner table this week.

Closer to home, four people have been charged with manslaughter in the October death of Winnipegger Kyle Andrew Devon Jerome. Winnipeg police haven't released full details yet, but expect this to work through the courts over the coming months.

On Winnipeg's roads, a rally this weekend called for safety changes after sixteen traffic deaths so far this year. Families and advocates gathered to say the city needs to act on intersection design and enforcement before the number climbs further. If you sit on any civic committees, expect this to come up at budget season.

Premier Wab Kinew told the NDP convention he wants to be remembered as Manitoba's best premier, not just its first First Nations one, as he looks toward re-election. Meanwhile, former PC leader Obby Khan says he'll sit in the legislature as an Independent, a notable shake-up on the opposition benches heading into that same election cycle.

Up north, Poplar River First Nation was locked down for more than a day after a man and a teenager allegedly shot at a residence and fled. The community is still dealing with the aftermath.

And on the watch list: Canada's Alert Ready system runs its twice-yearly nationwide test this Wednesday, November 18, hitting Manitoba phones, TVs, and radios at 1:55 p.m. local time. It's just a test, but expect your phone to buzz.

blocks.title: Carney says Canada could turn to Chinese automakers if Trump trade talks fail
blocks.script:
Mark Carney is wrapping up a nine day world tour in China today, and the headline from Beijing is blunt: Carney says Canada could turn to Chinese automakers and deepen ties with China if trade talks with Donald Trump keep stalling. That's a real shift in tone from a prime minister who spent much of this year trying to shore up the integrated North American auto sector. Conservative MP Stephanie Kusie called the broader tour a pattern of Liberal governments cozying up to state actors with shaky records on democracy and human rights, while Carney's team frames it as diversification, not retreat from Washington.

On the sidelines of that same trip, Carney held his first meeting with Quebec Premier Paul St-Pierre Plamondon since the provincial election. By all accounts it was cordial, no fireworks, but Quebec is still running its own outreach to Washington on trade, a reminder that provinces aren't waiting on Ottawa to manage the US file.

Back home, the Green Party has a new leader. Members elected former MP Mike Morrice, who's promising a focus on affordability alongside the party's usual fight with oil and gas companies.

blocks.script:
New research out today flips a long-standing assumption about heart aging. Per ScienceDaily, scientists found the heart doesn't age evenly across the muscle. Instead, inflammation and scarring cluster as hotspots in the valves and major blood vessels, not the heart muscle itself. That changes where researchers look for prevention strategies as you get older, and it's worth asking your cardiologist about valve and vessel health specifically, not just heart muscle function.

Separately, another ScienceDaily report: a common osteoporosis drug blocked spinal damage in zebrafish, preventing the mineral buildup linked to chronic back pain. It's early, animal-only research, but it points to a new genetic pathway behind spinal degeneration.

On the Canadian side, CBC reports flu season is arriving early this year in Alberta, which could strain hospital capacity there this winter.

blocks.title: Jets' Comeback, Raiders' Rookie Debut, Elks Win Cup
blocks.script:
Start with your Jets. Winnipeg rallied from a four-goal deficit on Saturday to beat the Chicago Blackhawks 5-4 in a shootout, their sixth straight win. Mark Scheifele had a goal and three assists and scored the shootout winner, and in doing so passed Dale Hawerchuk to become the franchise's all-time points leader with 933 career points. Kyle Connor and Gabriel Vilardi each had a goal and an assist as Winnipeg erased a 4-0 hole. The Jets host Ottawa on Tuesday.

Now the Raiders. Rookie quarterback Fernando Mendoza made his first National Football League start on Sunday at Allegiant Stadium, and Las Vegas lost 21-13 to the defending Super Bowl champion Seahawks. Mendoza opened with a rushing touchdown and a 10-7 halftime lead, but Seattle's defense sacked him six times and held him to 143 yards passing in the second half. Tight end Brock Bowers left with an ankle injury early and didn't return, which hurt Mendoza's options. Per ESPN, Drew Lock threw for 240 yards and two touchdowns to seal it. The Raiders try for Mendoza's first win next week in Denver.

Quick hits: the Edmonton Elks beat the Montreal Alouettes 37-30 to win the 113th Grey Cup, with Cody Fajardo named MVP. Canada beat Sweden to reach the women's world hockey final against the United States.

blocks.script:
Company & Economy Analysis, Evidence arsenal, lesson 9: Rebalancing: frequency, thresholds, and what the research shows.

Here's the number that surprises people: Vanguard's research on rebalancing, going back decades of market data, found almost no difference in long run returns between rebalancing monthly, quarterly, annually, or using a five percent threshold band. The spread between strategies was often under twenty basis points a year. That's the headline. Rebalancing is not a return engine. It's a risk control.

Here's the mechanism. Say you start at sixty percent equities, forty percent bonds. Equities run hard for three years, now you're at seventy-five, twenty-five. You haven't gotten richer in some permanent sense, you've gotten riskier. Your portfolio's volatility now looks like a seventy-five twenty-five mix, not the sixty forty you planned for. Rebalancing back to sixty forty sells some of what ran up, buys some of what lagged, and resets your risk to the level the plan called for. In the long run, because equities tend to outperform bonds, periodic rebalancing has sometimes meant a small long-run return drag, not a gain, because you're trimming the winner. The benefit is smoother volatility and a portfolio that still matches the client's actual risk tolerance, which is the thing that was agreed on in the first place.

The one mistake: people chase precision on timing. They debate monthly versus quarterly versus calendar-based versus threshold-based as if one of those unlocks extra return. It doesn't, within reason. The research point that matters is that having a rule and following it beats not having one, far more than which rule you pick. The failure mode isn't picking the wrong frequency, it's not rebalancing at all during a long bull run, because selling the winner feels wrong.

In Thomson ONE, if you want to show a client what drift looks like, pull the portfolio's current asset allocation versus the account's stated target, that's usually sitting in the account summary or portfolio analytics module.

Today's task below takes care of the practice.

Financial Planning Facts, lesson 35: Death of a spouse: the first year checklist.

When a spouse dies, the surviving spouse is often handed a stack of paperwork while grieving, and the tax and planning deadlines do not pause for that. Here is the one thing to understand today: in the year of death, there's a final tax return due, called the terminal return, and most registered assets can roll to the survivor tax free if the beneficiary designation or the estate structure is right. Get that rollover wrong and you create a tax bill that didn't need to exist.

Take a real example. David dies in 2026 with an RRIF worth 400,000 dollars and his wife Linda named as successor annuitant, not just beneficiary. Because she's named successor annuitant, the RRIF simply continues in her name. No deemed disposition, no tax on David's terminal return for that account. Compare that to a scenario where Linda was named only as beneficiary, not successor annuitant: the RRIF would still roll tax free to her as a qualifying survivor if she transfers it to her own RRSP or RRIF within the time allowed, but it requires an active transfer, paperwork, and a filing election. Miss that step and the full 400,000 gets added to David's terminal return as income, taxed in a single year at the highest brackets. In Manitoba in 2026, that pushes well past the top combined rate, over 50 percent on the upper portion. That's a six figure difference for missing a form.

The one mistake people make: assuming "it's a joint account, it just passes through automatically" without checking how each specific asset is titled. RRSPs, RRIFs, TFSAs, and the principal residence each have their own rules. TFSAs need a named "successor holder," not just beneficiary, for the tax free status to continue seamlessly. People conflate these designations and assume one phrase covers everything. It doesn't.

Also know the deadline shape: the terminal return is due April 30 of the year following death, or June 15 if the deceased had self employment income, though any tax owing is still due April 30.

Communication, lesson 35: Closing: asking for the decision without pressure.

There's a study out of Harvard Business School by Francesca Gino and her colleagues on what they call "the escalation of commitment" problem in sales conversations. The finding that matters here: the salespeople who closed the most deals weren't the ones who pushed hardest at the end. They were the ones who asked a plain question and then stopped talking. Silence did the closing, not pressure.

Here's what that looks like in practice. You've made your recommendation, you've answered the objections, and now you say: "Does this make sense to move forward, or is there something still unresolved?" Then you stop. Not "so what do you think, I mean obviously this is the right move, but no pressure." Just the question, then silence.

Worked example. You're advising a nonprofit board on a $40,000 fundraising campaign. You've laid out the plan, the risk, the timeline. The moment to close is: "Are you ready to approve this at today's vote, or do you need another week?" That's it. Two options, both acceptable, no stacking a third sentence on top of it. If you add "I really think this is the right call" after that question, you've just told them their answer should be yes before they've said anything, and board members notice that. It reads as pressure even when you don't mean it as pressure.

The one mistake: people keep talking after the ask. Chris Voss, the former FBI hostage negotiator, calls this "talking past the close." You ask the question, then out of nervousness you fill the silence with more selling. That second sentence is where trust leaks out, because it signals you didn't trust your own ask.

Financial Planning Facts: Pull one client file where a spouse predeceased the other, and confirm in writing whether RRSP, RRIF, and TFSA beneficiary designations said "successor" versus "beneficiary," and flag any mismatch for review.

Communication: In your next client or board conversation, write your closing question in advance, two sentences at most, and say it, then count five seconds of silence in your head before anyone else speaks.

blocks.label: The Ten
blocks.title: Cisco, RBC, OPG Lead Today's Company Talk
blocks.script:
Cisco leads the board today. The networking giant raised its full year revenue forecast, now guiding to between 74.8 billion and 75.8 billion dollars, up from a prior range of 72.2 billion to 73.4 billion, the Globe reports. The tailwind is obvious: data centre and AI networking demand is still accelerating. The headwind is valuation, a lot of that growth is already priced into the stock. An evidence based advisor tells a client this is a reason to own broad technology exposure, not to concentrate a portfolio around one AI infrastructure name.

Royal Bank of Canada is next. It's cutting senior climate finance roles as part of a restructuring, with that work shifting to a public policy unit run out of Washington, the Globe reports. The tailwind is cost discipline at a bank already posting strong earnings. The headwind is reputational, it reads as a retreat from climate commitments made publicly a few years ago. An advisor would say one reorganization doesn't change the investment case for a diversified, dividend paying bank stock.

Ottawa's bank watchdog is in the news too. The Globe's commentary argues the federal plan to sharpen anti money laundering oversight at the Office of the Superintendent of Financial Institutions might actually work, provided it gets real resources and becomes more transparent. The tailwind is restored confidence in bank compliance. The headwind is that past AML enforcement has been slow and underfunded. An advisor tells a worried client that regulatory tightening on banks is a governance story, not a reason to sell bank shares.

Ontario Power Generation is getting scrutiny over Darlington. The Globe details how the nuclear refurbishment ran nearly 13 billion dollars and 20 years, and asks whether more overhauls make sense. The tailwind is decades of reliable, emissions free baseload power once the work is done. The headwind is the track record on cost and timeline discipline. An advisor would flag this as a reason to hold utility exposure through diversified funds rather than betting on any single refurbishment project.
talkingPoints: Cisco's upgraded guidance shows AI networking demand is still real money, not just hype.
RBC trimming climate finance jobs is a cost story, watch if peers follow.
Darlington's 13 billion dollar, 20 year refurb is a cautionary tale for future nuclear bets.
The EDC-BDC merger could matter more for your exporting clients than your portfolio.
An NDA to see a condo price should make any buyer ask why.

blocks.title: Budget's New CCPC Capital Gains Break, RRIF Reform Push
blocks.script:
Start with the one change every incorporated business owner and physician on your book needs to hear about. Budget 2026 creates a new Canada Growth Incentive capital gains exemption worth up to fifteen million dollars per qualifying individual, per business, separate from the existing lifetime capital gains exemption which stays capped around one point two seven five million. The catch, this only applies to shares issued on or after budget day, November 5th, and the exemption excludes professional practices, consulting businesses, and anything principally dependent on an individual's skill or reputation, which likely rules out a lot of incorporated physicians and consultants directly. You can claim the new incentive or the old lifetime exemption on the same company's shares, not both, so any client structuring a sale or a share issuance now needs this modelled before they sign anything.

On RRIFs, the advocacy campaign to scrap mandatory minimum withdrawals isn't dying. Globe and Mail personal finance reports advisor Aaron Hector is pressing Ottawa again after the budget's RRSP and RRIF consolidation plan, arguing the government needs to actually fix the rules, not just reshuffle them. If clients ask why their RRIF minimum didn't change this year, that's why: nothing's locked in yet.

CIRO issued a technical bulletin revising the list of acceptable exchanges and market tiers across Canada and the U.S., plus a member bulletin flagging Security Financial Services and Investment Corp's intention to resign its CIRO membership, worth noting if any client holds accounts there.

Can't stack the new exemption with the lifetime capital gains exemption on the same shares, model both scenarios.

blocks.title: Hydro Review Calls, Health Violence, Fire in West Broadway
blocks.script:
Manitoba Hydro's three billion dollar gas turbine proposal out of Brandon is facing fresh pressure this morning. CBC Manitoba reports critics want the province to release the Public Utilities Board's recommendations before cabinet makes any final call, and the government is taking its time studying them before going public. If you've got clients with Hydro bonds or anyone watching provincial debt exposure, this is the one to track: a formal board review changes the timeline and the politics around a three billion dollar commitment.

At the Jamie Felix sentencing hearing, defence lawyers spent the day arguing their client showed a split, almost Jekyll and Hyde personality around the 2023 killing of five people, asking the judge for the minimum parole ineligibility period. The Crown is seeking twenty five years. Families of the victims gave gutting statements in court, and this hearing will likely run into next week.

Two of Manitoba's largest health-care unions are turning up the volume on workplace violence. The Free Press reports violence-related injury claims are up forty one per cent, and the unions want hospitals treated like high-risk industrial sites under labour law, not business as usual. For anyone on a hospital foundation board, expect this to come up at your next meeting.

The Winnipeg School Division is changing how report cards go out, holding them until after parent-teacher conferences so discussions happen before the grades land. CBC says it's the division's largest shift in that process in years.

A three storey apartment building in West Broadway caught fire Thursday morning, heavy smoke and flames from the top floor, one firefighter was hurt.

And that Microsoft outage you heard about earlier is still dragging into Winnipeg. Hospitals, schools and city offices running on Microsoft 365 and Outlook have had patchy email and Teams access since Thursday afternoon, so if you can't reach a contact at the Province or the WRHA today, that's likely why.

On the watch list: Manitoba Hydro, already covered above. The Winnipeg Blue Bombers are getting talked about too, with head coach Mike O'Shea citing inconsistency as the team's biggest issue this season.
